From 1965 to 1967, Lieutenant General Lewis Walt commanded every Marine in Vietnam — III Marine Amphibious Force — during the hardest years of the buildup. A decorated World War II and Korea veteran, Walt believed the war would be decided in the villages, and he pushed his Marines to protect the population as fiercely as they fought the enemy.

Under his command, the Marines pioneered pacification efforts that became models studied for decades. Walt never pretended the war was simple. He just insisted it be fought with both courage and conscience.

He led the Corps' largest combat command through its trial by fire, and he never asked his Marines to do anything he wouldn't do himself.

“BY 2030, POLAND WILL FIELD MORE TANKS THAN GERMANY, FRANCE, ITALY, AND BRITAIN COMBINED.”

While much of Western Europe spent the post-Cold War decades downsizing heavy armor divisions, Poland a nation of 38 million is executing the most ambitious conventional military buildup on the European continent.

By the end of the decade, the Polish Land Forces are projected to field an active arsenal of over 1,500 modern main battle tanks. For comparison, the combined tank fleets of the United Kingdom (~150), France (~220), Germany (~300), and Italy (~200) total fewer than 900 vehicles.

Key pillars behind Poland’s armored juggernaut:

Warsaw has acquired 366 U.S. Abrams tanks, including 250 factory-fresh M1A2 SEPv3 variants and 116 upgraded M1A1 FEP models to anchor heavy mechanized divisions along the eastern border.

A landmark agreement secures 1,000 K2 Black Panther tanks, consisting of 180 initial deliveries and 820 K2PL variants co-produced in Polish factories with localized reactive armor and active protection systems.

 Poland leads the entire NATO alliance in defense investment, dedicating over 4% of its GDP to military procurement and readiness.

The tank buildup is integrated with 96 Boeing AH-64E Apache Guardian attack helicopters, hundreds of HIMARS and K239 Chunmoo rocket launchers, and F-35A Lightning II stealth fighters.

 Poland is actively scaling its armed forces toward a target of 300,000 personnel, cementing its status as NATO’s primary conventional land bulwark on the Eastern Flank.

The center of gravity in European defense has permanently shifted east from the Rhine to the Vistula.

Lieutenant General Victor "Brute" Krulak saw the Vietnam War more clearly than almost anyone in Washington — and paid the price for saying so. As the Marines' leading counterinsurgency thinker, he argued the war would be won by protecting villages, not by body counts, and he built the Combined Action Program that put Marines to live and fight alongside Vietnamese villagers.

His warnings went unheeded, and the big-unit war ground on. But the Marines who served in the CAP program never forgot what Krulak understood: that the people were the prize, and that winning them mattered more than any statistic.

A warrior and a scholar, in an era that needed both.

U.S. Navy SEAL officers Leif Babin, Jocko Willink, and Seth Stone standing on the rooftop of "Full Metal Jacket," the combat outpost that SEAL Team 3’s Task Unit Bruiser called home during the Battle of Ramadi in 2006.

During that brutal deployment, Ramadi was the deadliest city on Earth. Under the tactical leadership of Commander Jocko Willink, with Babin leading Charlie Platoon and Stone commanding Delta Platoon, Task Unit Bruiser fought shoulder-to-shoulder with the U.S. Army and Marine Corps. Venturing deep into enemy-held territory night after night, they established sniper overwatch positions, engaged insurgents at point-blank range, and helped wrest the city back from al-Qaeda.

Their crucible produced some of the most decorated warriors in Naval Special Warfare history, including legendary sniper Chris Kyle, Michael Monsoor (who was posthumously awarded the Medal of Honor), and Ryan Job. Seth Stone himself earned two Silver Stars for conspicuous gallantry under fire, repeatedly putting his own life on the line to shield his teammates and direct airstrikes against overwhelming enemy forces.

Tragically, in September 2017, Stone was killed in a skydiving accident when his parachute failed to open after jumping from a hot air balloon. While his passing left an irreplaceable hole in the community, his humility, quiet professionalism, and ferocious warrior spirit continue to inspire every leader who learns from Bruiser’s legacy.

Leaders who took extreme ownership of every round, every life, and every mission.

Fair winds and following seas, Seth. The Only Easy Day Was Yesterday. 🇺🇸🔱⚡🦅

THE CAMP PENDLETON GRENADE PIT SACRIFICE  MARINE INSTRUCTOR THREW STUDENT TO SAFETY AND SHIELDED HIM FROM DEADLY BLAST

In an act of instantaneous courage at the School of Infantry-West, Marine combat instructor Staff Sgt. Brett Meil placed his own body directly over a live, ticking M67 fragmentation grenade to shield a panicked recruit, absorbing the blast to save a fellow Marine, as documented by Marines.mil and the USO.

For his extraordinary heroism in the face of death, Meil was awarded the Navy and Marine Corps Medal, the military’s highest non-combat decoration for valor.

The Split-Second Crucible in Pit Two
According to official Marine Corps accounts and reporting by Marine Corps Times, the entire incident unfolded in less than five seconds:

The Freeze Under Pressure: During a live-fire grenade qualification range at Camp Pendleton, California, an entry-level student Marine pulled the pin on an M67 grenade. When the safety lever unexpectedly released in his hand, the student froze in terror with the fuse actively burning.

 Recognizing the imminent catastrophe, Meil stepped directly into the danger zone, forcibly stripped the live munition from the student's locked grip, and physically vaulted both the recruit and himself over the concrete revetment wall.

After hitting the ground outside the bunker, Meil realized the armed grenade had bounced off the ledge and landed within the lethal casualty radius of their prone position. Without hesitation, Meil threw his entire torso over the young Marine to absorb the impact.

Surviving the Blast: The grenade detonated inches away, peppering Meil with dozens of high-velocity shrapnel wounds across his body while leaving his student with only minor injuries. Following emergency surgery, Meil made a complete recovery, resumed his duties training future infantrymen, and was named a 2024 USO Service Member of the Year.

How does Staff Sgt. Brett Meil’s selfless instinct to shield a recruit define the core ethos of the Marine Corps?

He received the Navy Cross. Marines still tell the story of Dong Ha as the standard for what one officer, alone and unafraid, can do.

CAPT. DANIEL REYNOLDS BECOMES FIRST U.S. SPACE FORCE GUARDIAN IN HISTORY TO EARN PRESTIGIOUS ARMY RANGER TAB

The feat cements Reynolds as the military’s first dual-tabbed "Space Ranger," having previously made history as the service’s first Guardian to conquer the Army’s grueling Sapper Leader Course, according to Space Training and Readiness Command.

Conquering the Army’s Toughest Leadership Crucible
Graduating from the military’s premier small-unit tactical course required enduring 62 days of mental and physical extremes across three demanding environments:

Darby & Mountain Phases: Enduring severe caloric restriction and sleep deprivation, Reynolds led combat patrols through the rugged elevation of the northern Georgia mountains, testing tactical planning under relentless physical stress.

Florida Swamp Phase: Navigating waterborne insertions and ambush scenarios through the dense waterways of coastal Florida, evaluating leadership while completely exhausted.

Bridging Ground & Space Domains: While Guardians manage satellite constellations, space domain awareness, and missile warning architectures, Reynolds demonstrated the vital importance of space professionals understanding the tactical realities and friction faced by frontline ground combat units.

SURROUNDED BY 300 TALIBAN AT COP KEATING, WOUNDED STAFF SGT. RALLIED COUNTERATTACK: CLINTON ROMESHA’S STAND FOR HIS MEN

At dawn on October 3, 2009, roughly 50 American soldiers defending Combat Outpost Keating—a remote, indefensible base situated at the bottom of a steep valley in eastern Afghanistan’s Nuristan Province—woke to a coordinated ambush by more than 300 heavily armed Taliban fighters raining down fire from the surrounding high ground.

During what became known as the Battle of Kamdesh, Section Leader Staff Sgt. Clinton Romesha of Bravo Troop, 3-61 Cavalry, 4th Brigade Combat Team, 4th Infantry Division, orchestrated a legendary defense recognized with the nation's highest military decoration, as documented by the U.S. Army and the Congressional Medal of Honor Society.

Gallantry Under Overwhelming Fire
According to his official Medal of Honor citation, Romesha’s actions prevented the outpost from being completely overrun:

Leading Through the Breach: After shrapnel from an RPG blast wounded his neck, shoulder, and arm, Romesha refused medical evacuation, immediately taking charge of the tactical counter-effort and moving through relentless direct machine-gun fire to rally isolated defenders.

Neutralizing High-Ground Positions: Operating without cover, Romesha utilized an array of weapons—firing an M4 carbine, taking up a fallen comrade’s sniper rifle, and employing an AT4 rocket launcher—to eliminate multiple enemy fighting positions and machine-gun bunkers.

Directing Devastating Close Air Support: Under sustained sniper fire, he calibrated target coordinates for incoming F-15E Strike Eagles, B-1B Lancers, and AH-64 Apache gunships, bringing ordnance dangerously close to friendly positions to decimate advancing Taliban waves.

The Stand for Fallen Brothers: As enemy fighters breached the perimeter, Romesha assembled a volunteer team of five soldiers, leading a push across 100 meters of exposed ground to recover the bodies of fallen teammates and secure the ammunition point so no American was left behind.

Eight American heroes made the ultimate sacrifice that day defending COP Keating: Staff Sgt. Justin Gallegos, Sgt. Christopher Griffin, Sgt. Joshua Kirk, Sgt. Michael Scusa, Spc. Stephan Mace, Spc. Kevin Thomson, Sgt. Vernon Martin, and Sgt. Joshua Hardt.

“OFF-DUTY AT AN OKINAWA GAS STATION, A U.S. MARINE HEARD A CRASH AND SPRANG INTO ACTION.”

On October 15, 2026, U.S. Marine Corps Sergeant Jacob L. Lyons had stopped at a gas station in Uruma, Okinawa, Japan, when the violent sound of a two-vehicle collision shattered the evening quiet.

He didn't hesitate. Sprinting toward the mangled wreckage, the off-duty Explosive Ordnance Disposal (EOD) technician with the 9th Engineer Support Battalion (Combat Logistics Regiment 37, 3rd Marine Logistics Group) found an elderly Japanese woman trapped inside her car, pinned hard against the steering wheel, in severe pain and distress.

What happened next represents the best of the American military community overseas:

Freeing the Trapped Driver: Lyons forced open the passenger-side door and, teaming up with a local Japanese bystander, manually forced the driver's seat rearward to relieve the crushing pressure on her chest and give her room to breathe.

Immediate Trauma Care: Lyons’ wife a former U.S. Navy Corpsman rushed over with another bystander to contact emergency dispatchers, providing immediate first aid and comforting the terrified driver through the language barrier.

Securing the Scene: Recognizing the danger of secondary collisions on the active roadway, Lyons stepped out into traffic, directing vehicles away from the wreckage and maintaining a clear access lane for incoming Japanese police and ambulances.

On October 23, 2026, at Camp Kinser, Colonel Robert Gerbracht presented Sergeant Lyons with the Navy and Marine Corps Achievement Medal for his swift life-saving actions.

“In a moment when another person's well-being was at stake, Sergeant Lyons did not hesitate,” said Col. Gerbracht. “He stepped forward with compassion, calm, and courage to help a member of our Okinawan community in need. His actions are a powerful reflection of our Marine Corps values and of the responsibility we carry as neighbors, partners, and guests in Japan.”

For Lyons, the motivation was simple:

“It was the right thing to do, not just as a Marine, but as a good person. Someone was in need and I was able to help, so I needed to.”

While the official war was fought in South Vietnam, Major General John K. Singlaub ran the war America wasn't supposed to be fighting. From 1966 to 1968, he commanded the Military Assistance Command's Studies and Observations Group — MACV-SOG — the Pentagon's covert unit running reconnaissance and rescue missions across Laos, Cambodia, and North Vietnam.

His teams operated in tiny groups, deep behind enemy lines, with casualty rates that defied belief. SOG's work stayed classified for decades, but its operators became legends: the quiet professionals who went where the maps said the war wasn't.

Singlaub never sought the spotlight. He just ran the hardest command of the war, in the shadows, and brought as many of his men home as he could.

On the night of November 21, 1970, fifty-nine-year-old Colonel Arthur "Bull" Simons led fifty-six Green Berets twenty-three miles into North Vietnam on one of the most daring raids in American military history. Their target: the Son Tay prison camp, where dozens of American POWs were believed held.

The raiders hit the camp with total surprise — only to find it empty. The prisoners had been moved months earlier. But the mission still shook Hanoi to its core: it proved no American was beyond reach, and word of the raid electrified POWs across North Vietnam, who began communicating, resisting, and holding on with new hope.

Simons, a legend of Army special operations, asked for nothing afterward. He had done what Green Berets do — gone where others wouldn't, for men he had never met.

“There are indications the aircraft began breaking up prior to impact. We may find parts of the aircraft some distance away from the actual impact site... We are asking anyone in the community who locates debris to contact local law enforcement immediately.”

Aerodynamic & Forensic Breakdown
The In-Flight Breakup Finding: During their initial media briefing in Palm Beach County, NTSB investigators confirmed that the Learjet 60 began shedding components prior to striking the ground, officially expanding the search radius across residential neighborhoods miles away from the primary impact crater.

The Missing Horizontal Stabilizer: Close-up frame analysis of civilian dashcam footage captured seconds before impact appears to show the aircraft's T-tail fuselage cleanly sheared off, missing the entire horizontal stabilizer and elevator assembly that controls aircraft pitch.

Why Loss of the Stabilizer is Fatal: On swept-wing, T-tail jets like the Learjet 60, the horizontal stabilizer generates continuous downward aerodynamic force to counter the natural forward center of gravity. If the stabilizer separates due to severe structural flutter, pitch trim runaway, or aerodynamic over-stress, the aircraft immediately lawn-darts into a near-vertical terminal dive that is physically impossible to pull out of, regardless of pilot yoke input.

The Escalating Mayday Telemetry: Flight tracking telemetry and ATC recordings show the crew encountered severe weather and icing while climbing through 8,700 feet. The aircraft suddenly entered an uncontrollable overspeed condition, with vertical descent rates accelerating from 10,000 FPM past 32,000 FPM before the violent ground collision.

Key Investigation Priorities for the NTSB
Locating the Empennage Components: Ground teams are prioritizing the recovery of tail structure fragments, elevator control horns, and pitch trim actuators to determine whether failure was aerodynamic, mechanical, or structural.

Analyzing Trim Jackscrew Position: Recovery crews will inspect the horizontal stabilizer trim actuator jackscrew to determine if an uncommanded runaway pitch condition preceded the structural separation.

Evaluating Atmospheric Stress & Icing: Meteorologists and investigators are analyzing weather radar data to evaluate whether severe convective turbulence or structural ice accumulation induced catastrophic aerodynamic loading at cruise altitude.

“Sorry, guys, I can't keep going.”

Those were the words of Lance Cpl. Brady A. Gustafson to the Marines in his vehicle as he was pulled away from his smoking machine gun minutes after his platoon was ambushed July 21, 2008, by withering enemy fire in Shewan, Afghanistan.

Nobody blamed Gustafson, 21, an infantryman with 2nd Platoon, Company G, 2nd Battalion, 7th Marine Regiment, for not being able to continue the fight, since the opening volley on the Marine mounted patrol included a rocket-propelled grenade that pierced the shell of the mine-resistant armor-protected vehicle in which Gustafson was manning the turret gun.

That RPG severed Gustafson's right leg, and yet he had the presence of mind to locate the enemy positions and place well-aimed machine gun fire on them, providing cover fire for the Marines in his platoon.

For his actions that day last year, Gustafson was awarded the Navy Cross and meritoriously promoted to corporal by Maj. Gen. Thomas D. Waldhauser, commanding general, 1st Marine Division, at a ceremony Mar. 27 at Lance Cpl. Torrey L. Gray Field at Marine Corps Air Ground Combat Center Twentynine Palms, Calif.
“What I like about today is that this is an opportunity to honor a Marine who had the humility, courage, presence of mind and camaraderie to keep going,” said Lt. Col. Richard D. Hall, the former commanding officer of 2nd Battalion, 7th Marines,
while they were deployed to Afghanistan in support of Operation Enduring Freedom – noting that Gustafson was more concerned about the welfare of his brother Marines than his own safety.
“He represents what is best about the human spirit. You can't buy that kind of human altruism.”

The Navy Cross is the highest honor specific to the Naval services and the second highest award in the U.S. military. Gustafson is just the 18th Marine to earn the award since the beginning of the Global War on Terror.

The Marines of 2nd Battalion, 7th Marines battled elements of Taliban and Islamist extremists in the Helmand and Farah provinces of Afghanistan.

Gustafson and Company G were patrolling in the village of Shewan, noted as a haven for insurgents, when they were ambushed from multiple positions by insurgents with RPGs and small-arms fire, according to the award citation for the Navy Cross.

After the RPG pierced the side of Gustafson's MRAP and struck him in the leg, causing the severe injury, he stayed focused and identified enemy firing positions, which he engaged with accurate machine-gun fire.

He noticed that the vehicle to his rear had become disabled by another RPG and instructed his MRAP driver to push the hobbled vehicle out of the “kill-zone.”

By doing so, Gustafson's MRAP became shrouded in fire. Through all this, Gustafson continued to direct fire at the enemy positions, suppressing their attacks and allowing the Marines to continue to engage the insurgents.

“Of every Marine I talked to, they all said if they had been hit in the leg with an RPG, the last thing they'd be thinking about is staying in the turret,” said 1st Lt. Andrew S. Bohn, 25, platoon commander of 2nd Plt., from Davis, Calif., and an occupant of the second vehicle that Gustafson directed to be pushed out of the line of fire.

Without that presence of mind, Bohn and the four other Marines from that vehicle may not have made it out of the ambush alive.

Only after firing more than 400 rounds, and reloading twice, did Gustafson permit combat aid-givers to remove him from the turret to apply medical treatment to his significant injuries. Lance Cpl. Cody Comstock, a member of Gustafson's platoon, applied his Combat Life Saver Course knowledge to the situation, wrapping a tourniquet around Gustafson's leg and dressing the wound while Gustafson was still in the turret.

“All of the lance corporals were going off their training in immediate action - nobody panicked,” said Bohn of his Marines. “There was a much-superior sized force attacking us, and there was only one (noncommissioned officer) in the platoon.”

After the action was over, Bohn recommended Gustafson for the Silver Star, the third highest combat award for valor, but Hall disagreed.

“My awards policy has always been strict (and) conservative,” said Hall, from Mankato, Minn. The former battalion commander noted that the deployment put all of his Marines in harsh conditions, and yet so many of the Marines excelled at operating at a high level that the “extraordinary became ordinary.”
Even so, Gustafson's actions were special.

“After reviewing what he did, even considering my awards policy and all the actions of 2nd Battalion, 7th Marines, it was easy, to me, to submit his award as a Navy Cross,” Hall said.

Gustafson, from Eagan, Minn., has a long road to recovery and walks with a pronounced limp on his prosthetic right leg. The fact he suffered traumatic injury made his family even more grateful for his return.

“(The Navy Cross) is the icing on the cake for us, but we know that Brady didn't do this for the awards,” said Rick Gustafson, father to the Marine hero and an Air Force retiree. “We're very thankful we have him here today. That's our primary emotion.”

According to his parents, Gustafson intends to buy a home in his native Minnesota and attend college somewhere near home.

“He recognizes the importance and honor of the award, but at the same time, he feels funny about being recognized,” said Gustafson's mother, Kim, about her son's quiet, unassuming manner and reluctance to stand in front of the hundreds of Marines, guests and media at the ceremony. “He was just fighting for
his guys' lives."

A comprehensive new defense survey and non-profit report have highlighted an alarming rise in food insecurity across the armed forces, revealing that an increasing number of junior enlisted households are relying on food banks and charitable assistance to make ends meet.   

Persistent inflation, surging off-base housing costs, and basic allowance for housing (BAH) shortfalls have severely squeezed junior enlisted paychecks, leaving many young military families unable to keep pace with everyday grocery and utility expenses. 

While the military provides comprehensive base pay and healthcare, lower-ranking service members (grades E-1 to E-4) often find themselves falling into financial vulnerability, particularly those with dependents stationed in high-cost-of-living areas. 

Charitable organizations, base relief societies, and local food distribution programs continue to step in to bridge the gap, sparking urgent renewed calls across Washington and the Pentagon for higher baseline compensation and structural pay reform for junior troops.

FORT BRAGG, N.C. (3/14/2011) – The 82nd Airborne "All-American" Divison commander presented the Distinguished Flying Cross to Chief Warrant Officer Carlos M. Roman, at Simmons Army Airfield, March 14, for his actions while serving in Afghanistan with the 3rd Combat Aviation Brigade.

Chief Warrant Officer Carlos M. Roman, a Fayetteville, N.C., native, is awarded a Distinguished Flying Cross by Maj. Gen. James L. Huggins, the commanding general of the 82nd Airborne Division, at Simmons Army Airfield, March 14, 2011.

Soldiers, family members and friends gathered to honor Roman, an AH-64D Apache helicopter pilot who now serves with the 1st Attack Reconnaissance Battalion, 82nd Combat Aviation Brigade, as Maj. Gen. James L. Huggins, the commanding general of the 82nd Airborne Division, pinned his award.

On Oct. 30, while deployed in support of Operation Enduring Freedom with the 3rd CAB, Roman answered the call for help in response to a close combat attack request in support of the ground troops of 2nd Battalion, 506th Infantry Regiment during a fire fight near Marga in eastern Afghanistan’s Paktika province. Instead of remaining at an altitude out of small arms range once they arrived at the scene of the attack, Roman and his crewmember descended in order to positively identify and engage the armed insurgents.

“I wasn’t scared, I just wanted to make sure I was shooting the right people,” said the Fayetteville, N.C., native.

His rapid response, superior situational awareness and exemplary airmanship resulted in the safe recovery of all friendly forces and successful destruction of more than 80 enemy personnel. His actions saved the lives of countless American soldiers and were critical in defeating the enemy.

“He answered in the most heroic way that a person could, putting his own self in harm’s way for the good of others,” Huggins said. “And, that’s about the noblest thing, I think, that can occur in mankind.”

Nobility is not the only virtue this pilot possesses, as he was rather humble about his prestigious award.

“I never fly for awards,” Roman said.

Perhaps this humility comes with the job.

“Ordinary people that do extraordinary things, that’s what this uniform is all about,” Huggins said.
